problem:
Given that $g(x)=3{x}^{4}-8{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+1$ is defined for $x\in (-8,8),$ find the values of $x$ for which the function is strictly decreasing.

$x\in (${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$)$

examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Intervals on Which a Function Is Decreasing Using Differentiation
examples.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x) = x^3 + x^2 - 8x$ is strictly decreasing.
examples.worked_solution:
To find where $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, we need to solve the inequality $f'(x) < 0.$

Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+2x-8,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+2x-8<0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
3(x + 2)\left(x -\dfrac 4 3\right) < 0,
$$

and the graph of $y=3(x+2)\left(x -\dfrac 4 3\right)$ has roots at $x=-2$ and $x=\dfrac 4 3,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/14e4f6078b21d209082c548f7f5d064abeaa98ee737aff919d2f6efad7a317e8.png)

The graph is negative on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right)$ between the roots, so we conclude that $f'(x) < 0$ on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right).$

Therefore, $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing on the interval $\left( -2, \dfrac{4}{3} \right).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/3f542d08fede8a5bad978b62bece12070b02e0d3b4369c804454356f07d0832a.png)

The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown above. The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=-3$ and $x=2.$ Given that ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at both $A$ and $B,$ find the intervals where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,-3) & -3 & (-3,2) & 2 & (2,\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ & \text{no extr.} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & + & 0 & +\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ on the intervals $(-3,2)$ and $(2,\infty ).$
